Dog Sitter or Boarding Kennel: Cost, Fit, and a Backup Plan

Weigh a dog sitter against a boarding kennel by cost, your dog's temperament, and safety. Includes a comparison worksheet and questions to ask providers.

Published: 2026-10-12Sources checked: 2Educational planning guide

A boarding kennel houses your dog at a facility with staff and other dogs, while a pet sitter cares for your dog in your own home; the better choice depends on your dog's temperament, the services offered, and having a reliable backup for when plans change.

What each option actually looks like

The two main ways to cover care while you travel differ in setting. According to the American Kennel Club, professional pet sitters can offer everything from dog walking to overnight stays at your house, and they are a strong fit for households with multiple animals, dogs with special needs, or owners who prefer their dog stay home. The AKC notes many dogs are less stressed following their normal routine at home, and that a home sitter avoids exposing your dog to other dogs and possible illness. It also distinguishes a professional sitter from the teenager down the street: a professional typically offers reliability, references, insurance, and a written agreement.

A boarding kennel, by contrast, houses your dog at a facility. The AKC's boarding guide describes good kennels as offering scheduled feeding, playtime grouped by compatibility, age, and energy level, and regular staff interaction, sometimes with extras like basic obedience practice or water play on hot days. It stresses that a reputable facility should let you tour every area your dog will access, including where meals are prepared, and that being refused a full tour is a reason to walk away.

Matching the choice to your dog

Temperament is the deciding factor. The AKC boarding guide notes many kennels offer, and some require, a trial run to assess how a dog handles the environment, including whether it struggles with separation anxiety or plays well with others. Some dogs thrive on the social bustle of a kennel; others do better staying home with a sitter. The AKC's advice for both settings converges on the same point: watch how your specific dog responds rather than assuming one option is universally better.

The AKC also points out that boarding facilities can accommodate dogs with health or behavioral considerations if you discuss those needs upfront, giving the example of a dog with arthritis that may need frequent breaks or joint supplements at mealtimes. Be transparent about issues such as separation anxiety, resource guarding, or a condition needing monitoring so the facility can plan for them. If your dog finds group settings stressful, our separation anxiety planning guide and daycare suitability guide can help you judge fit before you book.

A comparison worksheet

Prices depend on your area, your dog's size, and the services included, so gather quotes and fill this in rather than guessing. Compare the true total for the same trip length.

Include the backup line on purpose: a facility can fill up and a sitter can fall through, and having a reserve for a fallback keeps a surprise from derailing your trip. Compare the trip subtotals for the exact same dates and services rather than nightly rates in isolation, since add-ons like medication administration, extra walks, or a required trial run can change which option is actually cheaper for your dog. For dollar planning by dog size, pair this with our boarding cost by size guide and the five-year ownership cost framework.

Run a trial before the real trip

Both options reward a test run. The AKC boarding guide describes green flags after a trial stay: your dog comes home tired from healthy play, is free of cuts or bruises, shows no signs of distress such as excessive panting or drooling, has paws free of dried urine or feces, and is happy rather than merely relieved to see you. It frames the trial as a two-way test: the facility assesses whether your dog is a good fit, and you get to see whether your dog thrives while you are away. For a sitter, the AKC suggests hiring the person for a single day, going out, and observing how your dog seems when you return.

  1. Book a short trial well before your travel dates.
  2. Watch your dog's body language at drop-off and pickup.
  3. Check for any physical or behavioral changes afterward.
  4. Decide whether to proceed, adjust, or keep looking.

If your dog shows apprehension or you are unsure whether overnight stays suit them, the AKC's advice is simply to continue your search rather than force the arrangement. A trial is cheap insurance against a stressful trip for both of you.

Questions to ask each provider

For a boarding kennel, the AKC suggests asking:

  • Can I tour every area my dog will use, including where meals are prepared and where dogs play?
  • What immunization records do you require, and is a vet on staff or on call for emergencies?
  • How do you accommodate health conditions, and what are your sanitation practices for crates and communal areas?
  • How do you group dogs for play, and how do you handle a dog that prefers to be alone?

For a pet sitter, the AKC suggests asking:

  • Are you trained in pet CPR and first aid, and are you insured and bonded?
  • Can you provide client references and a written contract covering payment, cancellations, inclement weather, a veterinarian release, and an emergency contact?
  • How much exercise are you willing to give, and are you comfortable handling a dog of my dog's size?
  • Do you have a backup person if you cannot make it?

Why a backup plan is not optional

The AKC explicitly advises thinking about a backup: for a sitter, ask whether they have an alternate or business partner who can fill in during an emergency, and consider meeting that person too. Facilities can be fully booked or closed on your dates, and even a trusted sitter can get sick or face their own emergency. A single point of failure is exactly what you do not want when you are out of town, and lining up a second option before you leave costs you nothing but a little planning.

Line up a second option in advance so one cancellation does not leave your dog without care, and put your dog's essentials in writing for whoever steps in: feeding schedule and portions, medications, your vet's number and the nearest emergency clinic, and your dog's quirks. Keep the paperwork somewhere a substitute can find it; our vet record folder guide makes that easy, and our emergency fund formula helps you keep a small reserve for last-minute care.

Common mistakes when arranging care

  • Booking without a tour. The AKC warns to be wary of a kennel that will not show you the whole facility.
  • Skipping the trial run. It is the clearest read on whether your dog copes.
  • Comparing on price alone. Services, safety, and fit matter as much as the nightly rate.
  • Ignoring vaccination requirements. A kennel that does not ask for records is a red flag.
  • Having no backup. The AKC treats a fallback plan as essential.
  • Not being transparent about needs. Undisclosed anxiety, medication, or guarding can undermine an otherwise good fit.

What this guide cannot tell you

This guide cannot quote the nightly or per-visit rates in your area, because they vary by location, dog size, and the services you choose. It cannot judge which specific facility or sitter is right for your dog; only a tour, a trial run, and references can do that. It is not veterinary advice about your dog's health needs during a stay. Get quotes locally, tour facilities in person, check references, and talk with your veterinarian about any medical considerations before you travel.

FAQ

Is a pet sitter or a boarding kennel better for my dog?
It depends on your dog. The American Kennel Club notes many dogs are less stressed staying home with a sitter following their normal routine, which also avoids contact with other dogs. Others do well at a kennel with scheduled play and staff interaction. Temperament, special needs, and how your dog handles a trial run should guide the choice more than price alone.
What should I ask before choosing a boarding kennel?
The AKC recommends asking whether you can tour every area your dog will use, what immunization records are required, whether a veterinarian is on staff or on call, how they accommodate health conditions, and what sanitation practices they follow. Be wary of any facility that will not let you see the whole space or does not ask for vaccination records, which the AKC flags as a warning sign.
Why do I need a backup care plan?
Because plans fall through. The AKC advises asking a sitter whether they have an alternate or partner who can fill in during an emergency, and suggests meeting that person too. Boarding facilities can be fully booked or closed on your dates, and a sitter can get sick. Lining up a second option in advance keeps a single cancellation from leaving your dog without care.
